subject: chemistry
title: Oxidation numbers and redox equations
key_idea: An oxidation number tracks the electrons an atom has gained or lost, treating its bonds as ionic. Oxidation is electron loss and an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is electron gain and a decrease. Half-equations combine so that the electrons cancel.

blocks.text: An oxidation number is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic. This section covers the rules and how to use them.

items.meaning: The charge an atom would have if its bonds were 100% ionic. It is written as +2, −1 or 0.
Another name for oxidation number. The two terms mean the same.

items: An atom in an uncombined element has oxidation number 0, for example in Fe, O₂ and S₈.
The oxidation numbers in a neutral compound add up to 0.
The oxidation numbers in an ion add up to the charge on the ion.
Group 1 is always +1. Group 2 is always +2. Fluorine is always −1.
**Hydrogen** is +1, except in metal hydrides such as NaH, where it is −1.
**Oxygen** is −2, except in peroxides such as H₂O₂, where it is −1, and in OF₂, where it is +2.
Chlorine, bromine and iodine are −1 in compounds, except when combined with oxygen or fluorine.

items.text: Take the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻. The ion has a total charge of −2.
Oxygen is −2. Four oxygen atoms give 4 × (−2) = −8.
Let the oxidation number of sulfur be x. Then x + (−8) = −2, so x = +6.

diagram.alt: Practise finding the oxidation number of chlorine in a chlorine oxoanion.
diagram.question: A chlorine oxoanion contains one chlorine atom, **{n}** oxygen atoms and an overall charge of 1−. Oxygen is −2. Calculate the oxidation number of chlorine.
working: Let the oxidation number of chlorine be x. Then x + (−2 × {n}) = −1

items: Oxidation numbers in a compound add up to zero. In an ion they add up to its charge.
Oxygen is −2 and hydrogen is +1 unless the compound is a peroxide or a metal hydride.

sections.heading: Naming and writing formulae with oxidation numbers

blocks.text: A Roman numeral gives the oxidation number when an element can have more than one. This section covers how to name species and write formulae from the names.

items: The Roman numeral goes in brackets after the element name: iron(II) and iron(III), copper(I) and copper(II).
In an anion, the numeral goes after the stem: chlorate(I) is ClO⁻, chlorate(III) is ClO₂⁻ and chlorate(V) is ClO₃⁻.
Nitrate and sulfate with no numeral are taken to be NO₃⁻ and SO₄²⁻.
Use the numerals to write formulae by balancing charges: iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃, iron(II) oxide is FeO.
A Roman numeral shows the oxidation number. It gives a clear, unambiguous name.
Balance the total oxidation numbers to zero to write a formula from a name.

blocks.text: Redox reactions involve oxidation and reduction together. This section covers the two definitions and the terms that go with them.

items.meaning: Loss of electrons. The oxidation number increases.
Gain of electrons. The oxidation number decreases.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction both happen.
An electron acceptor. It oxidises another species and is itself reduced.
An electron donor. It reduces another species and is itself oxidised.

items: Metals generally form positive ions by losing electrons. Their oxidation number goes up.
Non-metals generally form negative ions by gaining electrons. Their oxidation number goes down.
These ideas apply to s-, p- and d-block elements, for example Mg, Al, Cl and Fe.
A change in oxidation number classifies a reaction. If no oxidation number changes, it is not a redox reaction.

blocks.text: Metals such as Mg, Al, Fe and Zn react with dilute acids to form a salt and hydrogen.

items: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Magnesium goes from 0 to +2 (oxidised). Hydrogen goes from +1 to 0 (reduced).
Fe + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂. Iron goes from 0 to +2.
The metal is the reducing agent. The acid, through H⁺, is the oxidising agent.

blocks.text: In a disproportionation reaction, one element in a single species is oxidised and reduced at the same time.

items: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
Chlorine goes from 0 to −1 in NaCl (reduced) and from 0 to +1 in NaClO (oxidised).
2Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺. Copper(I) goes to 0 and to +2.
Oxidation is electron loss and an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is the opposite.
The oxidising agent gains electrons. The reducing agent loses electrons.
In disproportionation the same element is both oxidised and reduced.

blocks.text: A half-equation shows either the oxidation or the reduction. Combining two of them gives the full redox equation, with the electrons cancelled.

items.text: Balance the atoms other than O and H first.
Add H₂O to the side that needs oxygen.
Add H⁺ to the side that needs hydrogen.
Add e⁻ so that the total charge is equal on both sides.
Multiply each half-equation so both involve the same number of electrons.
Add the two together and cancel the electrons and any H⁺ or H₂O on both sides.

blocks.text: Example: manganate(VII) oxidising iron(II) in acid solution.

items: Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O
Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻
Multiply the oxidation by 5, then add: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺

diagram.alt: A sequencing activity. Put the steps for building a redox equation in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps for building a full redox equation in order.
steps: Write each half-equation and balance the atoms other than O and H
Multiply so the electrons are equal

items: Balance atoms, then oxygen with H₂O, hydrogen with H⁺, then charge with e⁻.
The electrons in the two half-equations must be equal before you add them.

checks.q: State the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₄⁻ and of chromium in Cr₂O₇²⁻.
Explain, in terms of oxidation numbers, why the reaction Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O is a disproportionation.
checks.a: Chlorine goes from 0 to −1 in NaCl, so it is reduced. Chlorine goes from 0 to +1 in NaClO, so it is oxidised. The same element in one species is oxidised and reduced at the same time.

checks.q: Dichromate(VI) ions oxidise iron(II) ions in acid. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. Write the overall ionic equation.
checks.a: Multiply the iron half-equation by 6 and add: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O + 6Fe³⁺

items: Metals with acids can be s-, p- or d-block: Mg, Al, Fe and Zn. You write full equations, such as 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂. Ionic equations are not required here.
Reactions of metals with nitric acid or concentrated sulfuric acid do not give only a salt and hydrogen. They can be assessed as unfamiliar redox reactions.
For unfamiliar redox reactions, state which species gains electrons and which loses them, using oxidation numbers.

blocks.text: You use changes in oxidation number to balance equations that are hard to balance by inspection.

items.text: Work out the oxidation number of each element that changes.
Choose coefficients so that the total increase equals the total decrease.
Balance the other atoms, then O with H₂O and H with H⁺.

blocks.text: Example: MnO₄⁻ goes from +7 to +2, a decrease of 5. Fe²⁺ goes from +2 to +3, an increase of 1. So 1 MnO₄⁻ reacts with 5 Fe²⁺.
